- **Most likely diagnosis:** Nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome, also called Gorlin-Goltz syndrome, with multiple odontogenic keratocysts as the jaw manifestation.

- **Why this fits:** Multiple bilateral jaw radiolucencies, minimal bony expansion, palmar pits, and family history of early skin lesions strongly suggest a syndromic PTCH1-related condition.

- **Primary goals of the pathway:** Confirm the syndrome, establish the extent of jaw disease, preserve teeth and jaw development, reduce cyst recurrence, screen for associated neoplasms and anomalies, and organize lifelong surveillance.

- **Core team to assemble early:** Oral and maxillofacial surgeon, pediatric dentist, orthodontist, oral and maxillofacial radiologist, dermatologist, clinical geneticist/genetic counselor, pediatrician, and if needed neurology/neuro-oncology, gynecology, cardiology, ENT, and psychology.

- **First oral-maxillofacial step:** Obtain a full clinical dental and craniofacial assessment including tooth eruption disturbances, occlusion, swelling, pain, infection, paresthesia, and jaw expansion.

- **Initial imaging for jaw lesions:** Panoramic radiograph to map number, size, location, and relation of lesions to impacted or displaced teeth.

- **Advanced imaging for surgical planning:** Cone beam CT or CT to define cortical perforation, relation to inferior alveolar nerve, maxillary sinus/nasal floor involvement, and tooth displacement.

- **Need for tissue diagnosis:** Biopsy at time of initial decompression or enucleation to confirm odontogenic keratocyst histopathology and exclude other lesions.

- **Histologic expectation:** Parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelial lining with palisaded basal layer and corrugated luminal surface, often friable, supporting odontogenic keratocyst.

- **Diagnostic framework for the syndrome:** Use accepted major/minor criteria plus molecular confirmation when possible, rather than relying on jaw findings alone.

- **Major features to actively document:** Multiple odontogenic keratocysts, palmar or plantar pits, multiple basal cell carcinomas or very early basal cell carcinoma, calcification of the falx cerebri, and first-degree relative with the syndrome.

- **Additional phenotype screen:** Macrocephaly, frontal bossing, hypertelorism, cleft lip/palate, bifid or splayed ribs, vertebral anomalies, Sprengel deformity, syndactyly, ovarian fibroma, and cardiac fibroma.

- **Genetic testing plan:** Refer for germline testing of PTCH1 first, with SUFU considered if PTCH1 is negative or phenotype suggests it.

- **Why genetics matters:** Confirms diagnosis, guides family screening, affects medulloblastoma risk stratification, and supports lifelong surveillance planning.

- **Family pathway:** Offer genetic counseling and cascade testing to at-risk relatives because of autosomal dominant inheritance and variable expression.

- **Dermatology involvement:** Full skin examination at baseline to document existing lesions and educate on early basal cell carcinoma recognition.

- **Sun protection counseling:** Strict UV avoidance, protective clothing, sunscreen, and avoidance of tanning devices because radiation and UV can increase skin tumor burden.

- **Radiation caution:** Minimize ionizing radiation exposure whenever feasible, because these patients are radiation-sensitive and may develop numerous basal cell carcinomas in irradiated skin.

- **Brain tumor surveillance consideration:** Assess medulloblastoma risk with genetics input, especially if SUFU-related disease is suspected, as surveillance intensity may differ.

- **Neurologic pathway:** Baseline neurologic review and pediatric/neurology input if symptoms, developmental concerns, or genotype-specific brain tumor risk is present.

- **Female-specific pathway when relevant:** Gynecology review in adolescence/adulthood for ovarian fibroma surveillance and symptom awareness.

- **Cardiac consideration:** Cardiology review if symptoms, murmur, or phenotype raises concern for cardiac fibroma.

- **Chest/skeletal assessment:** Targeted evaluation for rib and vertebral anomalies if clinically indicated, avoiding unnecessary radiation-heavy imaging.

- **Dental developmental planning:** Coordinate with pediatric dentistry and orthodontics because cysts often disturb eruption, displace teeth, and complicate future alignment.

- **Principle of jaw lesion management in a 14-year-old:** Favor conservative, staged treatment where possible to preserve adjacent teeth, vital structures, and jaw growth.

- **When conservative treatment is especially useful:** Large cysts, lesions close to the inferior alveolar nerve, lesions around developing teeth, or multiple simultaneous lesions.

- **Conservative option 1:** Marsupialization or decompression to reduce cyst volume, thicken the lining, and make later definitive enucleation safer.

- **Conservative option 2:** Delayed secondary enucleation after shrinkage, often improving preservation of teeth and reducing morbidity.

- **Definitive surgery option:** Enucleation with careful removal of the friable lining once lesion size and anatomy permit.

- **Adjuncts to reduce recurrence:** Peripheral ostectomy and selected chemical curettage protocols may be considered in accessible lesions, balancing benefit against morbidity.

- **What to avoid in a child when possible:** Routine aggressive block resection, because it increases morbidity and is usually reserved for exceptional recurrent or destructive cases.

- **Tooth management principle:** Preserve involved permanent teeth whenever feasible, especially developing teeth, unless non-restorable, non-functional, or obstructing safe treatment.

- **Erupted/unerupted tooth decisions:** Teeth severely displaced may erupt after decompression; extraction is considered only if prognosis is poor or lesion clearance requires removal.

- **Infection control:** Manage any acute infection first with drainage if needed and appropriate antibiotics only when clinically indicated.

- **Pain and function:** Address analgesia, chewing difficulty, and oral hygiene limitations during the staged treatment period.

- **Surgical sequencing for multiple cysts:** Prioritize the largest, symptomatic, infected, rapidly enlarging, or high-risk lesions first, while monitoring smaller asymptomatic sites.

- **Documentation before intervention:** Record baseline sensory status, tooth vitality when relevant, occlusion, eruption stage, and radiographic measurements for each lesion.

- **Specimen handling:** Submit each lesion separately if anatomically distinct, because multiple lesions may differ in activity or pathology.

- **Recurrence counseling:** Explain that odontogenic keratocysts in this syndrome recur frequently and new cysts can also arise over time, so repeated treatments may be necessary.

- **Postoperative oral follow-up:** Regular reviews with clinical exam and interval panoramic imaging, with CBCT reserved for problem-solving or operative planning.

- **Imaging surveillance strategy:** Use the lowest-radiation modality compatible with the clinical question and avoid overly frequent CT-based studies.

- **Practical jaw surveillance interval:** Commonly annual or individualized radiographic follow-up during adolescence and early adulthood because new cysts are common in this period.

- **Long-term jaw surveillance:** Continue periodic monitoring lifelong, as syndromic odontogenic keratocysts may recur or appear later.

- **Orthodontic timing:** Delay or modify orthodontic treatment until jaw lesions are stabilized, because active cyst disease can alter eruption and root position.

- **Restorative and preventive dental care:** Intensify caries prevention, periodontal care, and fluoride use, since repeated surgery and altered eruption increase dental maintenance needs.

- **Psychological support:** Offer support for chronic disease burden, repeated procedures, cosmetic concerns, and anxiety related to cancer risk.

- **Education for patient and family:** Provide a written care plan describing the syndrome, warning signs of skin lesions, neurologic symptoms, jaw recurrence, and need for scheduled surveillance.

- **Red flags requiring urgent reassessment:** Rapid facial swelling, severe pain, pus discharge, numbness, trismus, visual or neurologic symptoms, or rapidly changing skin lesions.

- **How to formally confirm the diagnosis:** Combine clinical criteria, histopathologic confirmation of odontogenic keratocysts, characteristic systemic findings such as palmar pits, and germline molecular testing.

- **How to present the management plan to the family:** Explain that this is a hereditary syndrome with benign but recurrent jaw cysts and risk of other tumors, requiring coordinated lifelong care rather than one-time surgery.

- **A practical pathway summary:** Same-week OMFS and dermatology review, panoramic plus targeted CBCT, biopsy-confirming one representative lesion during decompression/enucleation, genetics referral for PTCH1/SUFU testing, pediatric screening for associated manifestations, staged conservative cyst management, and structured lifelong dental, skin, and syndrome surveillance.

- The likely condition is actinic cheilitis, a premalignant sun-induced disorder of the lower lip vermilion.
- The lower lip is affected most because it protrudes outward and receives more direct ultraviolet exposure than the upper lip.
- Chronic ultraviolet radiation, especially UVB, causes direct DNA injury in keratinocytes through formation of cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and other photoproducts.
- UVA also contributes by generating reactive oxygen species, which produce indirect oxidative DNA damage, lipid peroxidation, and protein injury.
- Repeated DNA damage overwhelms normal repair mechanisms, allowing accumulation of mutations in epithelial cells.
- UV-induced mutation of tumor suppressor genes, especially TP53, is a major step in development of epithelial dysplasia.
- Loss of normal p53 function reduces cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis, so damaged keratinocytes survive instead of being eliminated.
- Ultraviolet exposure also promotes abnormal proliferation of atypical basal and suprabasal keratinocytes.
- Chronic sun injury causes epithelial atrophy in some areas and hyperkeratosis in others, producing the persistent dry, rough, scaly clinical appearance.
- Solar elastosis develops in the underlying connective tissue because UV degrades collagen and alters elastic fibers through matrix metalloproteinase activation.
- UV radiation induces local immunosuppression, reducing immune surveillance against atypical or mutated cells.
- Chronic inflammation from repeated photodamage further supports progression by releasing cytokines and growth-promoting mediators.
- Over time, cumulative ultraviolet injury transforms normal vermilion epithelium into dysplastic epithelium characteristic of actinic cheilitis.
- Actinic cheilitis is clinically important because continued UV-driven genetic damage can progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the lip.

- **Most likely diagnosis:** Dentinogenesis imperfecta, most consistent with **Shields type II** if isolated, or **type I** if associated with osteogenesis imperfecta

- **Why this fits:**
  - Gray-brown, **opalescent teeth**
  - **Rapid attrition**
  - **Periapical radiolucencies in non-carious teeth**
  - Radiographic triad of **bulbous crowns**, **cervical constriction**, and **pulpal obliteration**
  - **Short roots** further support dentinogenesis imperfecta

- **Most likely pathophysiology:**
  - Abnormal dentin formation with weak dentinoenamel support
  - Enamel may be normal structurally but fractures away because of defective underlying dentin
  - Pulpal obliteration occurs from continued abnormal dentin deposition
  - Periapical lesions can occur due to pulpal degeneration/necrosis despite absence of caries

- **Key differential diagnoses to consider:**
  - **Dentin dysplasia type II**
    - Can show thistle-tube pulp changes rather than classic total obliteration and bulbous crowns
  - **Amelogenesis imperfecta**
    - Primarily enamel defect, not classic bulbous crowns/cervical constriction/pulp obliteration
  - **Fluorosis or tetracycline staining**
    - Discoloration without this radiographic pattern
  - **Regional odontodysplasia**
    - Usually localized, not generalized hereditary pattern
  - **Dentinogenesis imperfecta type III**
    - Rare; shell teeth pattern rather than pulpal obliteration is more characteristic

- **Essential history:**
  - **Family history** of similar teeth abnormalities
  - History of **bone fractures**, blue sclerae, hearing issues, joint laxity, or known **osteogenesis imperfecta**
  - Onset and rate of tooth wear
  - Pain, swelling, prior dental abscesses
  - Functional issues: mastication, sensitivity, esthetics
  - Previous restorations and failures

- **Clinical tests indicated:**
  - Full **intraoral examination** for extent of attrition, loss of vertical dimension, fractures, occlusion, and mobility
  - **Pulp sensibility testing**
    - May be unreliable because pulps are obliterated
  - **Percussion/palpation** for teeth with suspected apical disease
  - Periodontal charting and occlusal assessment
  - Photographic documentation for baseline

- **Radiographic tests indicated:**
  - **Panoramic radiograph**
    - Global overview of affected dentition and periapical lesions
  - **Full-mouth periapical series**
    - Best for root length, pulpal obliteration, and apical pathology
  - **Bitewings**
    - To assess coronal breakdown and remaining tooth structure
  - **CBCT** only if needed
    - For complex endodontic/surgical planning, unclear periapical lesions, or implant/prosthetic planning

- **Medical/genetic tests indicated:**
  - If isolated dental phenotype suspected: consider **DSPP gene testing**
  - If osteogenesis imperfecta features are present or suspected: referral for **medical/genetic evaluation**, including **COL1A1/COL1A2 testing**
  - If OI suspected: coordinate with physician for **skeletal assessment** and fracture history review
  - Genetic counseling is appropriate, especially if family history is positive

- **Biopsy/histology:**
  - Not routinely required for diagnosis
  - May be incidental if extracted teeth are sent for confirmation

- **Main treatment goals:**
  - Preserve remaining tooth structure
  - Prevent further attrition
  - Eliminate infection
  - Maintain function and occlusal vertical dimension
  - Improve esthetics
  - Provide long-term restorative stability

- **Staged management plan — Stage 1: urgent disease control**
  - Treat **symptomatic or infected periapical lesions**
  - Provide analgesia as needed
  - Address acute abscesses with drainage if indicated
  - Institute meticulous preventive program:
    - Fluoride toothpaste/varnish
    - Diet counseling
    - Non-abrasive home care
    - Nightguard only if appropriate after restorative planning and if parafunction is present

- **Stage 2: comprehensive diagnostic planning**
  - Determine which teeth are **restorable, endodontically treatable, or hopeless**
  - Assess extent of **vertical dimension loss**
  - Mount casts/digital occlusal analysis as needed for rehabilitation planning
  - Multidisciplinary planning with **prosthodontist, endodontist, oral surgeon**, and possibly **geneticist/physician**

- **Stage 3: protect remaining dentition**
  - Cover vulnerable posterior teeth with **full-coverage restorations** to reduce wear
  - In a young adult, consider **indirect onlays/crowns** or full-coverage crowns depending on remaining structure
  - Protect anterior teeth with **crowns/veneered full-coverage restorations** when indicated
  - Use adhesive approaches cautiously because bonding to abnormal dentin may be less predictable

- **Stage 4: endodontic management of teeth with periapical radiolucencies**
  - Attempt **root canal treatment** only when technically feasible
  - Expect difficulty because of **pulpal obliteration** and short roots
  - Use magnification and CBCT selectively for canal location
  - If nonsurgical endodontics is not feasible or prognosis is poor:
    - Consider **apical surgery** in selected cases
    - Otherwise **extraction** may be more predictable

- **Stage 5: extraction of hopeless teeth**
  - Extract teeth with:
    - Non-restorable crown destruction
    - Unmanageable infection
    - Vertical root fracture
    - Extremely short roots/poor periodontal or prosthetic prognosis
  - Send representative extracted teeth for pathology only if diagnosis is uncertain

- **Stage 6: definitive prosthetic rehabilitation**
  - Restore function and esthetics with a **full-mouth rehabilitation plan** if needed
  - Options depend on tooth prognosis:
    - Tooth-supported crowns/bridges
    - Overdentures
    - Removable partial dentures
    - Implant-supported restorations after growth is complete and bone/medical status are suitable
  - Re-establish or preserve **vertical dimension** carefully and incrementally

- **Special considerations for this 18-year-old:**
  - At 18, definitive prosthodontic planning is reasonable, but growth status should still be confirmed before implants
  - Esthetic concerns are often significant and should be addressed early
  - Long-term restorability may be limited by short roots and dentin weakness
  - Treatment may need transitional restorations before definitive rehabilitation

- **Restorative cautions:**
  - Avoid relying on large direct restorations alone in heavily affected teeth
  - Crown retention may be compromised by **cervical constriction** and altered dentin
  - Ferrule may be limited
  - Endodontically treated teeth may have guarded prognosis because roots are short and canals are calcified

- **Follow-up plan:**
  - Frequent recalls, typically **every 3–6 months**
  - Monitor:
    - New periapical pathology
    - Progression of attrition
    - Restoration failure
    - Occlusal changes
    - Periodontal status
  - Repeat periapical imaging as clinically indicated

- **Prognosis:**
  - Guarded for severely affected teeth
  - Better when diagnosed early and protected with full-coverage restorations before major attrition occurs
  - Long-term success often depends on coordinated multidisciplinary rehabilitation

- **Bottom line:**
  - The picture is classic for **dentinogenesis imperfecta**
  - Indicated tests are **comprehensive dental imaging, limited sensibility/periapical assessment, family/medical evaluation, and genetic testing when appropriate**
  - Management should be **staged: control infection, protect teeth from further wear, treat or remove teeth with apical disease, and complete definitive prosthetic rehabilitation with long-term monitoring**

- In the esthetic zone, use the wax-up and surgical guide to place gingival margins symmetrically and proportionately.

- Allow adequate healing time after esthetic crown lengthening, commonly about 6–12 weeks for preliminary reassessment and often closer to 3–6 months before final anterior restorative margins, especially in a high smile line.

- **Radiographs as tolerated:** assess bone levels, eruption status, caries, and local contributing factors while minimizing distress.

- **Immediate oral hygiene phase:** intensive professional supragingival/subgingival debridement as tolerated, frequent maintenance, and parent-supervised toothbrushing instruction.

- **Home care advice:** soft small-headed toothbrush, twice-daily brushing with fluoridated toothpaste, gentle gumline cleaning, and age-appropriate interdental cleaning where possible.

- **Antimicrobial support:** consider short-term **chlorhexidine** only if the child can use it safely and the transplant team agrees; avoid prolonged use and alcohol-containing products.

- **Caries prevention:** fluoride varnish, diet counseling, and management of food stagnation sites to reduce additional morbidity.

- **Pain/bleeding control:** optimize hygiene and debridement first; use local measures for bleeding; for analgesia prefer **paracetamol/acetaminophen within transplant-team-approved dosing**.

- **Medication modification can be decisive:** if the child is on **cyclosporine**, discuss with the transplant physician whether switching to **tacrolimus** or adjusting the regimen is safe, as this can reduce recurrence and severity.

- **If a calcium-channel blocker is present:** ask the medical team whether an alternative antihypertensive can be substituted, since these drugs can worsen overgrowth.

- **Do not change immunosuppression independently:** all adjustments must be made only by the transplant team because rejection prevention takes priority.

- **Re-evaluation interval:** review after initial hygiene phase, typically within a few weeks, to assess reduction in inflammation, bleeding, and functional improvement.

- **Indications for surgery:** persistent fibrotic enlargement after optimal plaque control and medical review, especially when chewing, tooth eruption, speech, hygiene access, or esthetics remain significantly impaired.

- **Surgical options:** gingivectomy and/or flap recontouring depending on tissue thickness, pocket architecture, and need for access.

- **Timing of surgery:** proceed only when the child is medically stable, blood results are acceptable, and the transplant team confirms no contraindication.

- **Antibiotic strategy:** do **not** use routine prophylaxis solely for transplant history unless specifically indicated by the medical team or another condition; if antibiotics are needed therapeutically, check interactions carefully.

- **Parent counseling:** explain that recurrence is common if plaque control is poor or if the causative medication must continue, so long-term maintenance is essential.

- **Peri-implant mucositis** = inflammatory lesion confined to the soft tissues around an implant, with **bleeding on probing/suppuration possible**, **clinical signs of inflammation**, but **no progressive supporting bone loss beyond initial physiologic remodeling**.

- **Peri-implantitis** = inflammatory lesion around an implant with **bleeding on probing and/or suppuration**, **increased probing depths compared with prior exams**, and **progressive crestal bone loss** after initial remodeling.

- **Periodontitis affecting a tooth** = inflammatory disease of the tooth-supporting tissues with **clinical attachment loss**, **periodontal pocketing/recession**, and **radiographic alveolar bone loss** at a **tooth**, not an implant.

- **First distinction: implant vs tooth** = peri-implant diseases occur around an **implant fixture**; periodontitis occurs around a **natural tooth with periodontal ligament**.

- **Key feature separating mucositis from peri-implantitis** = **bone loss** attributable to disease is **absent in mucositis** and **present in peri-implantitis**.

- **Both mucositis and peri-implantitis can show** = redness, swelling, bleeding on gentle probing, tenderness, and sometimes suppuration, so **soft-tissue inflammation alone is not enough** to diagnose peri-implantitis.

- **Peri-implant mucositis diagnosis relies on** = clinical inflammation around the implant plus **stable radiographic bone levels** relative to baseline after expected early remodeling.

- **Peri-implantitis diagnosis relies on** = clinical inflammation plus **radiographic bone loss** and usually **deepening of peri-implant probing depths** over time.

- **If baseline implant records are available** = diagnose peri-implantitis when there is **bleeding/suppuration on probing**, **increased probing depth**, and **bone loss beyond prior post-restoration levels**.

- **If baseline implant records are unavailable** = peri-implantitis is generally supported by **bleeding/suppuration on probing**, **probing depth ≥ 6 mm**, and **bone level ≥ 3 mm apical to the most coronal intraosseous part of the implant**.

- **Periodontitis around a tooth is distinguished by attachment apparatus anatomy** = teeth have a **periodontal ligament**, so they can show **clinical attachment loss** and mobility patterns different from implants.

- **Probing interpretation differs** = increased probing depth around a tooth suggests periodontal pocketing with attachment loss; around an implant it may reflect mucosal inflammation, prosthetic contour issues, or true peri-implant tissue breakdown, so **radiographs and prior measurements are essential**.

- **Bleeding on probing is important but nonspecific** = it indicates inflammation in gingivitis, mucositis, peri-implantitis, and periodontitis, but **does not by itself distinguish among them**.

- **Suppuration increases concern for destructive disease** = it may occur in peri-implantitis or periodontitis, but can occasionally be present with severe mucosal inflammation, so **bone/attachment loss must still be assessed**.

- **Radiographic pattern helps** = peri-implantitis shows **crestal bone loss around the implant**; periodontitis shows **alveolar bone loss around the tooth root**; mucositis shows **no additional implant bone loss**.

- **Expected early implant remodeling must not be overcalled as peri-implantitis** = some crestal bone change may occur after placement/loading, so diagnosis requires **loss beyond physiologic remodeling**.

- **Gingivitis on adjacent teeth does not equal peri-implantitis** = a patient may have **gingivitis at teeth** and **peri-implant mucositis at implants** simultaneously, each without destructive bone loss.

- **Gingivitis vs periodontitis at adjacent teeth** = gingivitis has **bleeding/inflammation without attachment loss or radiographic bone loss**; periodontitis has **attachment loss and bone loss**.

- **Clinical workflow for distinction** = identify whether the site is a tooth or implant, record **bleeding/suppuration**, measure **probing depths**, compare with prior exams, and review **radiographs for bone levels**.

- **Most likely diagnosis around an inflamed implant with adjacent gingivitis** = **peri-implant mucositis** if the implant shows inflammation but **no progressive bone loss**; **peri-implantitis** only if there is accompanying **pathologic bone loss**.

- **Most likely dental diagnosis:** spontaneous pulp necrosis with chronic apical abscesses in structurally abnormal, caries-free teeth associated with familial hypophosphatemic rickets.

- **Why this happens:** hypophosphatemic rickets can cause defective dentin mineralization, enlarged pulp chambers with pulp horns extending close to the enamel-dentin junction, interglobular dentin, microcracks, and easy bacterial ingress even without caries.

- **Overall management principle:** coordinate dental infection control with medical/endocrine optimization because persistent systemic phosphate dysregulation increases risk of recurrent dental pathology and impaired mineralization.

- **Core team members:** pediatric dentist, endodontist, oral and maxillofacial surgeon if extractions are needed, pediatric endocrinologist/metabolic bone specialist, pediatrician, and orthodontist if dentofacial growth issues are present.

- **Immediate dental priorities:** identify all infected teeth, drain acute infections if present, eliminate sinus tract sources, relieve pain, and prevent spread of odontogenic infection.

- **Initial history points:** FHXR subtype if known, current therapy regimen, adherence, timing of doses, previous abscesses, history of spontaneous dental pain, prior endodontic treatment, family history, growth history, orthopedic issues, and any history of craniosynostosis or hearing problems.

- **Medication review:** document phosphate supplementation, active vitamin D analogs such as calcitriol/alfacalcidol, and whether the child is receiving burosumab, because treatment type affects biochemical targets and dental preventive planning.

- **Clinical dental examination:** assess all molars and incisors for sinus tracts, tenderness, swelling, mobility, wear, enamel cracks, developmental defects, occlusion, oral hygiene, plaque retention, and any delayed eruption or malocclusion.

- **Pulp testing:** use sensibility tests cautiously because results in children can be unreliable, but compare suspect teeth with controls to support diagnosis.

- **Sinus tract tracing:** insert a gutta-percha cone into each sinus tract and obtain a radiograph to identify the responsible tooth.

- **Required dental imaging:** periapical radiographs of all suspicious teeth to detect widened periodontal ligament spaces, loss of lamina dura, rarefaction, atypical pulp morphology, and root development status.

- **Additional imaging:** panoramic radiograph to screen for multiple lesions, unerupted teeth, taurodontism-like appearance, root abnormalities, and generalized alveolar bone effects.

- **If findings are complex:** consider limited-field CBCT for persistent/recurrent lesions, unusual anatomy, cortical perforation, or surgical planning, while keeping radiation as low as reasonably achievable.

- **Assessment of tooth structure:** look for large pulp chambers, prominent pulp horns, thin dentin, and cracks or attrition that may justify preventive sealing or full coronal protection.

- **Primary differential diagnoses to exclude:** occult caries, dens invaginatus, molar-incisor hypomineralization, traumatic pulp necrosis, vertical crack, localized periodontal abscess, and other inherited dentin defects.

- **Microbiologic testing:** usually not required routinely, but consider if infection is unusually aggressive, recurrent despite adequate treatment, or the child is immunocompromised.

- **Dental treatment for restorable permanent molars:** conventional root canal treatment is usually indicated for necrotic teeth with periapical pathology.

- **Endodontic considerations:** expect complex pulp morphology, thin dentinal walls, and open apices in immature teeth; treatment may require apexification or regenerative endodontic procedures depending on root development.

- **If strategic tooth prognosis is poor:** extraction may be preferable when severe structural compromise, non-restorability, extensive bone loss, or repeated endodontic failure is present.

- **Space management after extraction:** involve pediatric dentist/orthodontist early to preserve arch integrity and plan eruption guidance.

- **Management of sinus tracts:** sinus tracts usually resolve after definitive treatment of the source tooth; persistent tracts after treatment require reassessment for missed canals, fracture, or another source.

- **Antibiotics:** not routinely indicated for chronic draining sinus tracts alone; use only when there is systemic involvement, spreading cellulitis, fever, diffuse swelling, or immunocompromise.

- **Pain/infection support:** provide appropriate analgesia, drainage if fluctuant swelling is present, and urgent care if airway risk or rapidly spreading infection develops.

- **Preventive restorative strategy:** seal pits and fissures early, restore attritional defects promptly, and consider protective full-coverage restorations for teeth with repeated microexposure risk.

- **Fluoride strategy:** high-fluoride toothpaste if age-appropriate and risk-based, topical fluoride varnish applications, and individualized remineralization support.

- **Oral hygiene support:** intensive plaque control, dietary counseling to reduce cariogenic challenge, and regular recall because any breach in enamel/dentin may accelerate pulpal infection.

- **Recall interval:** short recall, often every 3–4 months initially, to monitor for new abscesses, sinus tracts, and integrity of sealants/restorations.

- **Systemic investigations to request/confirm with endocrinology:** serum phosphate, calcium, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone, creatinine, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and where relevant 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.

- **Renal monitoring:** urinary calcium and phosphate handling, and renal ultrasound if indicated, because conventional therapy can contribute to hypercalciuria/nephrocalcinosis and treatment adjustments may be needed.

- **Disease-control assessment:** determine whether systemic therapy is adequately controlling phosphate wasting, because poor biochemical control is associated with ongoing mineralization defects.

- **Growth and skeletal review:** assess height/growth velocity, limb deformity status, bone pain, mobility, and orthopedic interventions, since these reflect overall disease control.

- **Craniofacial assessment:** evaluate for maxillary constriction, Class III tendency, delayed eruption, enlarged pulp chambers, taurodontism, and possible effects of craniosynostosis on facial growth.

- **Endocrine coordination question:** ask whether current regimen is optimized and whether persistent hypophosphatemia, secondary/tertiary hyperparathyroidism, or treatment complications are present.

- **If on conventional phosphate plus active vitamin D:** endocrinology should review adherence, dosing frequency, biochemical response, and parathyroid status.

- **If on burosumab:** confirm schedule, trough biochemical response, and whether systemic control has improved since initiation, while recognizing dental disease may still persist from preexisting structural defects.

- **Communication to medical team:** report that multiple periapical lesions in caries-free teeth strongly suggest dentin/pulp consequences of hypophosphatemic rickets rather than simple hygiene-related decay.

- **Communication to dental team:** emphasize that absence of caries does not exclude pulp necrosis in FHXR and that all suspect teeth require vitality/infection assessment.

- **Histories for recurrence risk:** previous recurrent abscesses in primary or permanent teeth, timing of onset relative to systemic treatment, and whether dental lesions preceded diagnosis or treatment optimization.

- **Family counseling point:** recurrent dental abscesses are part of the disease phenotype and do not necessarily reflect neglect or high sugar intake.

- **Prognosis discussion:** outcomes improve with early diagnosis, prompt endodontic/restorative care, rigorous prevention, and better systemic metabolic control, but recurrence in other teeth remains possible.

- **School/quality-of-life support:** address pain, missed school, eating difficulties, and psychosocial impact of repeated infections and dental treatment.

- **Long-term dental surveillance:** monitor both erupted and erupting teeth because newly erupted permanent teeth may later develop pulp necrosis despite appearing sound.

- **Orthodontic timing:** defer elective orthodontic forces on infected or recently treated teeth until infection is resolved and prognosis is clear.

- **If generalized pulpal risk is high:** consider pre-emptive sealing/protective restorations on susceptible molars soon after eruption.

- **Documentation:** chart all sinus tracts, radiolucencies, pulp status, restorability, root maturity, and systemic treatment status to allow coordinated follow-up.

- **Practical investigation set at first visit:** clinical exam, vitality/sensibility testing, sinus tract tracing, periapicals of affected teeth, panoramic radiograph, and direct communication with endocrinology for current biochemical results and treatment summary.

- **Practical multidisciplinary plan:** stabilize dental infections first, complete endodontic or extraction-based management of all involved teeth, institute aggressive prevention and close recall, and in parallel have endocrinology reassess metabolic control and treatment adequacy.

- Likely diagnosis: enamel-renal syndrome, most commonly due to biallelic FAM20A variants
- Key triad here: generalized enamel agenesis/hypoplastic AI, delayed/failed eruption with gingival fibromatosis, and nephrocalcinosis
- Strong family history supports an inherited autosomal recessive condition and need for family-wide assessment

- Core MDT should include paediatric dentistry, restorative dentistry/prosthodontics, orthodontics, periodontics, oral surgery, dental genetics/clinical genetics, paediatrics, and paediatric nephrology
- Add dental radiology, oral medicine/pathology if gingival biopsy is needed, dietetics if oral intake is limited by sensitivity, and psychology if quality of life is significantly affected

- Immediate priorities: pain/sensitivity control, prevention of further tooth surface loss, improvement of function/nutrition, and renal safeguarding
- Baseline photos, study models or digital scans, and full-mouth charting are important for monitoring progression and planning staged care

- Detailed history should document:
- Onset and severity of sensitivity
- Difficulty eating, brushing, and sleeping
- Previous eruption delay or failed eruption
- Family pedigree across multiple generations
- Renal history, UTIs, stones, haematuria, polyuria, growth concerns, medications
- Previous dental treatment tolerance and anaesthetic history

- Clinical examination should assess:
- Extent of enamel absence and exposed dentine
- Vertical dimension, attrition, fractures, pulpal symptoms
- Plaque control and caries risk
- Gingival enlargement distribution and impact on eruption
- Occlusion, space loss, and retained primary teeth
- Signs of infection, abscess, or sinus tracts
- TMJ symptoms and psychosocial impact

- Key dental investigations:
- Panoramic radiograph to assess eruption, impactions, pulpal calcifications, root form, and missing teeth
- Periapicals/bitewings as tolerated for caries, periapical status, and coronal anatomy
- Consider CBCT only if justified for impacted teeth/oral surgery planning
- Intraoral photographs and scans/models for occlusal planning
- Periodontal charting if gingival overgrowth is significant

- Typical radiographic features to look for in enamel-renal syndrome:
- Generalized very thin or absent enamel
- Unerupted or impacted teeth
- Intra-pulpal calcifications
- Hyperplastic dental follicles
- Coronal/resorption abnormalities and eruption disturbances

- Key medical investigations:
- Renal ultrasound to assess nephrocalcinosis/nephrolithiasis burden
- Serum U&Es, creatinine, eGFR, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate, magnesium, PTH, and vitamin D
- Urinalysis and urine calcium/creatinine ratio
- Nephrology review for long-term surveillance and management of renal complications

- Genetic investigations:
- Clinical genetics referral with counselling
- Targeted AI/enamel-renal syndrome panel or FAM20A testing
- Consider cascade testing for siblings/affected relatives
- Genetic confirmation helps prognosis, family planning, and coordinated renal screening

- Consider histopathology only if diagnosis is uncertain or tissue is removed during gingivectomy
- Gingival tissue in enamel-renal syndrome often shows fibromatosis-like changes and ectopic calcifications

- Preventive strategy from first visit:
- High-fluoride toothpaste appropriate to age/risk under specialist supervision
- Fluoride varnish applications at regular intervals
- Desensitising agents and possibly CPP-ACP if suitable
- Soft toothbrush, non-abrasive toothpaste, and tailored brushing instruction
- Dietary counselling to reduce erosive/acidic exposures and support adequate nutrition
- Preventive recalls usually every 3 months initially

- Immediate symptom control:
- Cover exposed dentine early with GIC/resin-modified GIC, composite sealants, or interim full coronal coverage where feasible
- Prioritise first permanent molars and incisors if these are the most symptomatic/functional teeth
- Use local anaesthesia carefully; hypersensitive teeth may require staged acclimatisation and behavioural support
- Consider inhalation sedation or GA for extensive care in a highly symptomatic/anxious child

- Stage 1 oral management: stabilisation
- Intensive prevention and sensitivity control
- Remove plaque-retentive factors and treat acute infection
- Place protective restorations to reduce pain and allow eating/brushing
- Stainless steel crowns on erupted permanent molars are often useful interim restorations in children
- Composite/GIC veneers or strip/composite build-ups may help anterior sensitivity and appearance
- Maintain as much tooth tissue as possible with minimal intervention

- Stage 2 oral management: periodontal/eruption management
- Periodontal assessment of fibrotic gingiva and its effect on eruption and hygiene
- Gingivectomy/gingivoplasty may be indicated if overgrowth causes pain, pseudo-pockets, hygiene failure, or blocks eruption/access
- Oral surgery input for exposure of impacted teeth is selective and based on realistic eruptive potential
- Recurrence of gingival overgrowth can occur, so surgery should be timed to functional need

- Orthodontic planning points:
- Early orthodontic intervention is often limited by poor enamel for bonding and altered eruption
- Avoid routine bonding to severely defective surfaces unless protected/restored first
- Orthodontic traction of impacted teeth may have guarded prognosis in enamel-renal syndrome
- Focus initially on space management, monitoring eruption, and coordinated planning with surgery/restorative teams

- Stage 3 oral management: restorative rehabilitation through adolescence
- Aim to preserve vitality and tooth structure until growth is near completion
- Replace failing interim restorations with more durable adhesive restorations as cooperation and eruption improve
- Posterior teeth may need indirect/onlay-type coverage when feasible
- Anterior teeth may require composite buildups for aesthetics, function, and psychosocial benefit
- Endodontics only if clearly indicated by symptoms/pathology; avoid unnecessary pulp risk in small abnormal crowns

- Stage 4 oral management: definitive post-growth rehabilitation
- Reassess once facial growth and eruption are sufficiently complete
- Definitive options may include full-mouth adhesive/onlay/crown rehabilitation depending on tooth substrate and periodontal status
- Implant planning, if needed, should be delayed until growth completion and coordinated with bone/eruption status
- Long-term prosthodontic planning should be conservative because patients often have complex eruption and periodontal issues

- Extraction decisions should be cautious:
- Extract only teeth with non-restorable breakdown, persistent infection, or hopeless eruption prognosis
- Account for future restorative and orthodontic implications before removing impacted or retained teeth
- Coordinate any extraction plan with nephrology if there are medical issues affecting perioperative care

- Anaesthetic and perioperative considerations:
- Check renal status before GA/sedation and avoid nephrotoxic medication where possible
- Liaise with nephrology regarding hydration, analgesics, and any metabolic abnormalities
- Prefer paracetamol-based pain strategies; NSAID use may need caution depending on renal function

- Follow-up structure:
- Paediatric dentistry-led reviews every 3 months initially
- Periodontal reviews according to gingival status
- Nephrology surveillance at intervals determined by renal findings
- Annual MDT reassessment of eruption, restorability, occlusion, and psychosocial needs

- Prognostic counselling:
- Condition is chronic and requires long-term staged care rather than one-time correction
- Sensitivity and appearance can usually be improved significantly with early protective treatment
- Gingival enlargement and eruption problems may recur or persist
- Renal monitoring is essential even if current kidney symptoms are mild

- Family counselling points:
- Recommend dental and renal screening for affected siblings/relatives
- Explain inheritance pattern and availability of genetic counselling
- Provide realistic expectations regarding repeated maintenance, restoration replacement, and possible future definitive rehabilitation

- Practical staged pathway summary:
- Visit 1: paediatric dental assessment, pain control, prevention, baseline records, urgent protective restorations, nephrology/genetics referrals
- Early phase: panoramic radiograph, renal work-up, genetic testing, regular fluoride/desensitising regimen, interim molar crowns/anterior coverage
- Intermediate phase: periodontal surgery if needed, selective oral surgery for eruption issues, monitor spaces and occlusion with orthodontic input
- Adolescent phase: transition from interim to more durable restorations while preserving tooth tissue and vitality
- Post-growth phase: definitive multidisciplinary restorative/prosthodontic rehabilitation with continued renal surveillance

- Sound enamel shows relatively strong natural autofluorescence.
- As mineral content decreases, enamel autofluorescence decreases.
- Demineralization increases light scattering, which reduces the emitted fluorescence signal from enamel.
- Therefore, early carious enamel typically appears darker or less fluorescent than sound enamel in autofluorescence-based detection.

- Do not proceed with extraction based on dental findings alone because easy bruising raises concern for thrombocytopenia and/or coagulopathy.

- Recognize key transplant-related risks:

  - Possible impaired hepatic synthetic function affecting coagulation.
  - Possible drug-related thrombocytopenia or marrow suppression.
  - Potential hypertension, renal dysfunction, and adrenal suppression depending on medications.

- Obtain a focused medical history before scheduling:
  - Date and indication for liver transplant.
  - Current graft status and most recent transplant follow-up.
  - Current medications with doses and timing, especially tacrolimus, cyclosporine, mycophenolate, sirolimus, steroids, valganciclovir, TMP-SMX, aspirin, or other anticoagulant/antiplatelet drugs.
  - History of rejection episodes, recent infections, hospitalizations, fever, malaise, bleeding, epistaxis, petechiae, gingival bleeding, melena, or prolonged bleeding after minor injuries.
  - Any history of neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, abnormal INR/PT/PTT, or prior transfusions.
  - Allergies and prior anesthetic/sedation issues.

  - Assess facial swelling, cellulitis, trismus, airway risk, and severity of odontogenic infection.
  - Check for petechiae, ecchymoses, jaundice, pallor, oral ulceration, candidiasis, and generalized gingival bleeding.
  - Record blood pressure, pulse, temperature, and weight.

  - Recurrent abscesses make extraction necessary.
  - If there is spreading infection, fever, dysphagia, dehydration, or systemic toxicity, arrange urgent hospital-based management.

- Essential laboratory work-up close to the procedure date:
  - CBC with differential.
  - Platelet count.
  - PT/INR.
  - aPTT.
  - Liver function panel if not recently available.
  - Renal function if sedation, nephrotoxic drugs, or medication adjustments are being considered.

- Interpret labs conservatively in collaboration with the medical team:
  - Defer elective office extraction if platelet count is low, INR is elevated, ANC is significantly reduced, or liver function is unstable.
  - Easy bruising plus abnormal labs may require correction before extraction.

- Practical hemostatic thresholds commonly used for dental extraction:
  - Platelets ideally > 75,000–100,000/µL for routine extraction in a child with transplant history.
  - Platelets < 50,000/µL generally require hospital management and likely hematology-guided support.
  - INR should be near normal; an elevated INR requires physician-directed correction and hospital planning.
  - Significant neutropenia increases infection risk and may alter timing and antibiotic strategy.

- Use a setting with immediate access to:

  - Understand antibiotics are adjunctive and do not replace extraction.

  - Liver transplant alone is not an indication.
  - Give prophylaxis only if another qualifying cardiac condition exists.

- Confirm whether the transplant team recommends antibiotic prophylaxis because of severe immunosuppression or neutropenia:
  - This is not automatic for all transplant patients.
  - Decision should be individualized with the medical team.

- Avoid empiric drug choices that interact with calcineurin inhibitors unless approved:
  - Macrolides such as erythromycin and clarithromycin can raise tacrolimus/cyclosporine levels.
  - Azole antifungals can also significantly interact.
  - NSAIDs may worsen renal function and bleeding risk.

- Preferred analgesic plan:
  - Acetaminophen in medically approved pediatric dosing, accounting for liver status and transplant team advice.
  - Avoid ibuprofen/NSAIDs unless specifically cleared because of bleeding and renal concerns.

- Local anesthetic strategy:
  - Local anesthesia is preferred if behavior allows.
  - Standard pediatric local anesthetics can be used in appropriate doses.
  - Use vasoconstrictor cautiously but it is usually acceptable unless specific contraindications exist.

- Sedation strategy:
  - Minimal sedation only if clearly necessary and medically cleared.
  - Deeper sedation/general anesthesia is better performed in hospital because hepatic metabolism, drug interactions, and airway/infection issues increase risk.

- Plan atraumatic extraction:
  - Minimize flap reflection and tissue trauma.
  - Gentle luxation and delivery.
  - Thorough debridement of infected granulation tissue.
  - Remove sharp bone only if necessary.
  - Avoid excessive surgical duration.

- Prepare local hemostatic measures before starting:
  - Pressure packs.
  - Resorbable gelatin sponge/collagen plug/cellulose.
  - Sutures.
  - Tranexamic acid mouthwash or topical application if recommended by the medical team and age-appropriate.

- Use primary local hemostasis routinely in this child even if labs are acceptable:
  - Place local hemostatic material in the socket.
  - Suture the site for soft tissue closure and clot protection.
  - Maintain firm pressure after extraction.

- If platelet count or coagulation is borderline but extraction is still necessary:
  - Perform only in hospital after physician-directed optimization.
  - Consider preprocedure platelet transfusion or coagulation factor support only under hematology/transplant guidance.

- If severe neutropenia is present:
  - Defer non-emergent extraction until medically optimized if possible.
  - If extraction is urgent because of active infection, do it in hospital with physician-directed antimicrobial support.

- Check morning-of-procedure status:
  - No fever or signs of systemic deterioration.

- **Why this is most likely:**

  - Thermal sensitivity to cold and hot is present.
  - No percussion pain, making symptomatic apical periodontitis unlikely.
  - Bite feels normal, so high occlusion is less likely as the main cause.
  - Very short timeline of 5 days favors a transient pulpal inflammatory response.

- **Important differential diagnoses to rule out:**
  - Hyperocclusion causing periodontal ligament inflammation.
  - Cement washout / exposed dentin at crown margin.
  - Open margin or microleakage.
  - Cracked tooth / cusp.
  - Irreversible pulpitis developing under the crown.
  - Residual caries or pulpal trauma from tooth preparation.
  - Referred pain from adjacent tooth or maxillary sinus source.

- **Immediate management:**
  - Reassure the patient that mild-to-moderate thermal sensitivity for days to a few weeks after crown cementation can occur.
  - Advise avoidance of very cold, very hot, and sweet stimuli temporarily.
  - Prescribe/advise analgesics if needed, such as NSAIDs if not contraindicated.
  - Check and adjust occlusion even if the patient reports it feels normal, because subtle prematurities may still contribute.
  - Inspect crown margins and cement excess; remove any residual excess cement if present.
  - If sensitivity is localized to exposed root/cervical margin, consider desensitizing agent/varnish.
  - Review in a short interval, typically 1–2 weeks, unless symptoms worsen sooner.

- **Definitive management if findings support reversible pulpitis only:**
  - Observation and monitoring.
  - Occlusal adjustment if any prematurity is detected.
  - Margin refinement / management of cement-related irritation if present.
  - Desensitizing treatment if marginal dentin exposure is identified.
  - Continue follow-up until symptoms resolve.

- **Definitive management if symptoms indicate irreversible pulpitis or progression:**
  - Endodontic treatment through the crown if the tooth becomes symptomatic with lingering thermal pain/spontaneous pain.
  - If the crown has defective margins, poor fit, or significant leakage, endodontic treatment may need to be combined with crown replacement depending on restorability and crown quality.

- **Features that would shift diagnosis toward symptomatic irreversible pulpitis:**
  - Pain that lingers after cold/hot stimulus is removed.
  - Spontaneous pain.
  - Increasing intensity or frequency of pain.
  - Night pain.
  - Need for analgesics with limited relief.
  - Progression despite occlusal adjustment and observation.

- **Clinical tests to perform:**
  - Detailed pain history:
    - Onset relative to crown cementation.
    - Whether pain is provoked only or spontaneous.
    - Duration of pain after thermal stimulus removal.
    - Whether hot worsens and cold relieves.
    - Presence of night pain.
    - Trend: improving, stable, or worsening.
  - Percussion test:
    - Vertical and lateral percussion on the crowned tooth and adjacent teeth.
  - Palpation:
    - Buccal vestibule and apical area for tenderness/swelling.
  - Occlusal examination:
    - Articulating paper in maximum intercuspation and excursions.
    - Check for heavy contacts on functional and nonfunctional cusps.
  - Thermal pulp testing:
    - Cold test on the crowned tooth if possible and compare with contralateral/adjacent control teeth.
    - Heat test if history suggests heat sensitivity and diagnosis remains unclear.
  - Electric pulp test:
    - Limited reliability through a full-coverage PFM crown, but may be attempted on exposed tooth structure if accessible or compared with adjacent teeth.
  - Bite test:
    - Tooth Slooth/cotton roll to detect crack-related pain on biting or release.
  - Periodontal examination:
    - Probing depths around the crown.
    - Check for isolated deep pocket suggestive of crack/root fracture.
    - Assess mobility.
  - Marginal evaluation:
    - Explorer assessment of crown margins for open margin, overhang, exposed dentin, or cement remnants.
  - Radiographs:
    - Periapical radiograph to assess periapical status, remaining dentin/restoration depth, cement excess, and possible periodontal ligament widening.
    - Bitewing if needed to evaluate crown margin adaptation and recurrent caries/open margin.
  - Transillumination if crack is suspected.
  - Selective anesthesia only if pain source localization is uncertain.

- **How test results guide treatment:**
  - Normal percussion/palpation, normal radiograph, brief non-lingering thermal response, and no occlusal issue:
    - Monitor as reversible pulpitis.
  - Heavy occlusal contact with tenderness developing on biting:
    - Adjust occlusion and review.
  - Defective/open margin, exposed dentin, or cement problem:
    - Correct local cause; monitor pulpal response.
  - Lingering thermal pain or spontaneous pain with normal periapical findings:
    - Diagnose symptomatic irreversible pulpitis and plan root canal treatment.
  - Percussion/palpation tenderness or apical radiographic changes:
    - Consider apical involvement and manage endodontically.
  - Positive bite-test/release pain or isolated deep probing:
    - Investigate crack; prognosis and treatment depend on crack extent.

- **Most likely practical plan today:**
  - Take focused pain history.
  - Perform percussion, palpation, thermal assessment, bite test, periodontal probing, and occlusal analysis.
  - Take a periapical radiograph.
  - Adjust occlusion if any prematurity is found.
  - Check crown margins/cement remnants.
  - If pain is stimulus-dependent and non-lingering with otherwise normal findings, diagnose reversible pulpitis and review in 1–2 weeks.
  - If pain lingers or is spontaneous, proceed toward endodontic treatment diagnosis and consent.

- Desquamative gingivitis is a clinical pattern, not a diagnosis; common autoimmune causes include mucous membrane pemphigoid, pemphigus vulgaris, and oral lichen planus/lichenoid disease.

- These disorders can look very similar clinically but require different prognosis assessment, medical workup, and treatment intensity.

- Perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence helps identify in vivo tissue-bound immune deposits and the pattern of deposition.

- Direct immunofluorescence can distinguish key entities:
  - Linear basement membrane zone staining suggests pemphigoid.
  - Intercellular epithelial staining suggests pemphigus vulgaris.
  - Fibrinogen/shaggy basement membrane zone patterns may support lichenoid disease.

- The biopsy should be taken from perilesional tissue rather than the ulcer base because intact epithelium is needed to preserve diagnostic immunoreactants.

- Ulcerated or heavily inflamed tissue often gives nondiagnostic or false-negative results because the epithelium and immune deposits may be destroyed.

- Establishing a definitive diagnosis before treatment improves clinicopathologic correlation and avoids mislabeling the disease.

- Empiric corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive therapy started before biopsy can reduce or alter immune deposition, lowering direct immunofluorescence sensitivity and obscuring diagnosis.

- A confirmed diagnosis is important because some diseases, especially mucous membrane pemphigoid, may involve extraoral sites such as the eyes and can lead to scarring and serious morbidity.

- Early identification of pemphigus vulgaris is critical because it can be potentially life-threatening and often requires prompt systemic therapy.

- Accurate diagnosis guides appropriate referrals, such as ophthalmology, dermatology, or oral medicine/oral pathology.

- Direct immunofluorescence also helps rule out mimicking conditions and supports selection of the safest, most effective long-term therapy.

- Therefore, perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence should be performed before empiric therapy whenever feasible to maximize diagnostic yield and guide management correctly.

- **Keystone pathogen concept:** *Porphyromonas gingivalis* can cause disproportionately large ecological and inflammatory effects despite being present at low abundance.

- **Around implants, health depends on symbiosis:** stable peri-implant tissues require a balanced biofilm and a controlled host immune response.

- ***P. gingivalis* disrupts this balance by inducing dysbiosis:** it remodels the local microbial community so that a more proteolytic, anaerobic, inflammation-loving biofilm becomes established.

- **It acts as an inflammophilic organism:** it benefits from inflammation because tissue breakdown products, peptides, and heme released in inflamed sites support its growth and that of other pathobionts.

- **Its virulence factors are central to this shift:** major factors include gingiproteases, fimbriae, lipopolysaccharide with atypical signaling behavior, outer membrane vesicles, and capsule.

- **Gingipains are especially important:** these cysteine proteases degrade host structural proteins, immunoglobulins, complement components, cytokines, and cell-surface receptors.

- **Immune subversion is a hallmark:** *P. gingivalis* does not simply trigger inflammation; it rewires host defenses so bacterial clearance is impaired while destructive inflammation persists.

- **Complement manipulation is a key mechanism:** it can alter complement activity, especially involving C5a signaling, producing inflammatory signaling while weakening effective killing.

- **TLR crosstalk is exploited:** interaction with Toll-like receptors, especially TLR2, can be skewed so leukocytes become inflammatory but less bactericidal.

- **Neutrophil function becomes dysregulated:** neutrophils are recruited and activated, yet chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and killing can be impaired, allowing biofilm persistence.

- **Macrophage responses are distorted:** macrophages may produce inflammatory mediators but show altered bacterial clearance and prolonged tissue-damaging activation states.

- **Adaptive immunity is also affected:** antigen presentation and lymphocyte responses can be shifted in ways that favor chronicity rather than resolution.

- **Barrier integrity is compromised:** epithelial junctions and soft-tissue attachment can be weakened, increasing microbial ingress and host exposure to biofilm products.

- **Peri-implant tissues may be particularly vulnerable:** compared with the periodontium around teeth, implants have different vascular supply, connective tissue fiber orientation, and attachment architecture, reducing resilience to inflammatory challenge.

- **Titanium surfaces provide a non-shedding substrate for biofilm maturation:** once dysbiosis is established on implant surfaces, microbial persistence is facilitated.

- **Surface roughness and microtopography can enhance plaque retention:** this can help organisms such as *P. gingivalis* integrate into a pathogenic consortium.

- **A polymicrobial synergy develops:** *P. gingivalis* cooperates with other anaerobes, increasing total virulence beyond what a single species could achieve alone.

- **This is the PSD model:** polymicrobial synergy and dysbiosis explains how a keystone pathogen reshapes the community to a disease-promoting state.

- **Inflammation drives tissue destruction through host mediators:** elevated IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, prostaglandins, and matrix metalloproteinases promote collagen breakdown and soft-tissue damage.

- **Bone loss is host-mediated as well:** inflammatory signaling increases RANKL and osteoclast activation, promoting peri-implant bone resorption.

- **The biofilm–inflammation loop becomes self-sustaining:** more inflammation creates more nutrient release, which supports more dysbiosis, which drives more inflammation.

- **Clinically, this destabilization shifts peri-implant mucositis toward peri-implantitis:** reversible soft-tissue inflammation can progress to irreversible supporting bone loss.

- **Even low levels of *P. gingivalis* can matter:** disease potential lies less in abundance alone and more in its capacity to reprogram host–microbe interactions.

- **In summary:** *P. gingivalis* destabilizes peri-implant homeostasis by promoting dysbiosis, subverting immune clearance, maintaining non-resolving inflammation, and thereby driving connective tissue breakdown and crestal bone loss.

- **Primary goal:** eliminate all active oral infection and minimize risk of bacteremia, bleeding, and peri-/post-transplant infectious complications before immunosuppression.

- **Overall timing target:** complete definitive dental treatment ideally **2–4 weeks before transplantation**, with earlier intervention for any acute infection.

- **Immediate multidisciplinary coordination:** involve **pediatric dentist, oral surgeon/hospital dentistry team, transplant hepatologist, transplant surgeon, pediatric anesthesiologist, primary pediatrician, and hematology/transfusion support if needed**.

- **First step:** contact the transplant team **before any invasive dental care** to confirm urgency, medical stability, and transplant timeline.

- **Medical information to obtain from transplant team:** diagnosis/severity of liver disease, current medications, history of varices/ascites/encephalopathy, prior bleeding episodes, infection history, central line status, allergies, nutritional status, and planned transplant date.

- **Key recent labs to request/review:** **CBC with platelet count, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen if available, liver function tests, renal function, glucose, and any transplant-specific infectious markers**.

- **Assess bleeding risk carefully:** end-stage liver disease may cause **thrombocytopenia, reduced clotting factor synthesis, platelet dysfunction, and hyperfibrinolysis**.

- **Assess anesthetic/sedation risk carefully:** hepatic dysfunction alters metabolism of sedatives/analgesics and may increase risk from deep sedation or general anesthesia.

- **Dental evaluation should be urgent:** perform comprehensive exam with **radiographs as tolerated** to identify all caries, non-restorable teeth, abscesses, furcation/periapical pathology, retained roots, and soft-tissue infection.

- **Prioritize treatment by infection risk:** treat **abscessed teeth, teeth with pulpal necrosis, cellulitis, swelling, fistulae, advanced periodontal infection, and non-restorable carious teeth first**.

- **Tooth with abscessed primary molar:** extraction is generally preferred over pulpal therapy if the tooth is non-restorable or close to exfoliation, because **elimination of infection source is the clearance objective**.

- **Deep carious primary teeth:** restore only if prognosis is predictable and treatment can be completed promptly; **extract teeth with questionable prognosis** rather than leaving possible future infection before immunosuppression.

- **Endodontic/pulp therapy decision-making:** avoid multi-visit or uncertain pulpal treatment when transplant is imminent; favor **single-visit definitive care or extraction**.

- **Hospital-based setting is preferred** if there is significant coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, poor cooperation, extensive treatment need, severe liver disease, or need for advanced monitoring.

- **Single comprehensive treatment session is often optimal** to reduce repeated bacteremia, reduce stress, and ensure complete clearance before transplant.

- **If the child is stable and cooperative with acceptable hemostatic profile:** selected care may be done with local anesthesia in an outpatient dental/hospital dental setting.

- **If sedation or general anesthesia is needed:** this should be planned jointly with **pediatric anesthesia and hepatology**, ideally in a tertiary pediatric hospital.

- **Avoid assuming routine office sedation is safe:** many sedatives are hepatically metabolized, and liver disease can increase risk of oversedation, delayed recovery, and encephalopathy.

- **Antibiotics are adjunctive, not definitive treatment:** dental abscess requires **drainage/extraction/restoration as indicated**; antibiotics alone do not equal clearance.

- **Use antibiotics when indicated for spreading infection, systemic signs, or inability to provide immediate source control.**

- **Antibiotic selection should be coordinated with hepatology/pharmacy:** choose agents with attention to **hepatic dosing, drug interactions, and renal status**.

- **Do not use hepatotoxic medications casually:** confirm all prescriptions with transplant/hepatology team.

- **Analgesia plan:** avoid or strictly limit drugs problematic in liver disease; **acetaminophen only if hepatology approves and within reduced dosing**, and **avoid NSAIDs** because of bleeding/renal risks unless specifically cleared.

- **Local anesthesia is generally useful and should include excellent local hemostatic planning** for invasive care.

- **Before extraction or surgery:** define thresholds for proceeding based on **platelet count and INR** per local hospital/transplant protocol.

- **If coagulation parameters are unacceptable:** coordinate **pre-procedure correction** as advised by hepatology/hematology, such as **platelet transfusion, plasma products, vitamin K if appropriate, or other factor/hemostatic support**.

- **Local hemostatic measures should be routine for extractions:** pressure, sutures, gelatin sponge/collagen plug/cellulose dressing, tranexamic acid mouthwash or topical use if approved, and close post-op observation.

- **Document baseline oral bleeding history:** epistaxis, easy bruising, prolonged bleeding after minor trauma, petechiae, or prior surgical bleeding.

- **Assess for oral manifestations of liver disease:** jaundice, petechiae, spontaneous gingival bleeding, candidiasis, angular cheilitis, poor oral hygiene, enamel defects, and malnutrition-related mucosal changes.

- **Screen for active systemic infection signs:** fever, facial swelling, trismus, lymphadenopathy, cellulitis, dehydration, poor intake, or lethargy.

- **If acute spreading odontogenic infection is present:** expedite **same-day hospital management** with drainage/extraction and medical support.

- **Infective endocarditis prophylaxis is not required unless there is a separate cardiac indication**; liver transplant candidacy alone is not an indication.

- **Central venous line presence alone does not justify dental antibiotic prophylaxis**, but line infection risk reinforces the need to remove oral infection foci quickly.

- **Oral hygiene stabilization is part of clearance:** institute supervised **twice-daily fluoride toothpaste brushing**, floss/interdental cleaning as feasible, and caregiver-assisted plaque control.

- **Topical fluoride should be provided:** fluoride varnish and high-caries-risk prevention plan to reduce new lesions before and after transplant.

- **Diet counseling is essential:** reduce frequency of fermentable carbohydrates, optimize hydration and nutrition, and coordinate with dietitian if the child uses high-calorie medical diets.

- **If candidiasis or other mucosal infection is present:** treat before transplant and verify resolution.

- **Obtain informed consent with family discussion of competing risks:** untreated dental infection vs bleeding/anesthesia risks vs transplant timing.

- **Recommended pathway timeline:**
  - **Week 0:** urgent dental-hospital/transplant joint review, exam, radiographs, labs, and treatment planning.
  - **Week 0–1:** manage any acute abscess/infection immediately; start antibiotics only if indicated; arrange OR/hospital slot if needed.
  - **Week 1–2:** complete definitive treatment for abscessed molar and all non-restorable/high-risk teeth; restore teeth with good prognosis.
  - **Week 2–4:** reassess healing, address any residual caries/plaque issues, reinforce prevention.
  - **At least 1–2 weeks before transplant:** provide final dental clearance letter if all infection is eradicated and healing is satisfactory.

- **Clearance criteria should include:** no untreated odontogenic infection, no draining sinus, no facial swelling, no teeth with hopeless prognosis left in situ, stable post-extraction healing, and prevention plan in place.

- **Dental clearance letter should document:** diagnoses, procedures performed, medications prescribed, hemostatic issues/management, healing status, residual noninfectious findings if any, and whether the child is currently free of active oral infection.

- **If complete clearance cannot be achieved before transplant:** clearly communicate unresolved foci and relative risk to transplant team so timing and peri-transplant antibiotic/monitoring plans can be adjusted.

- **Post-treatment follow-up is essential:** review within **7–14 days** after invasive treatment to confirm hemostasis, absence of infection, and adequate healing.

- **Post-transplant planning should begin now:** arrange close preventive recall because immunosuppression increases importance of meticulous oral hygiene and early management of new disease.

- **Practical management choice for this case:** prioritize **urgent extraction of the abscessed primary molar**, eliminate other non-restorable deep carious teeth, restore any salvageable lesions promptly, and complete care in a **hospital-based multidisciplinary setting** with up-to-date coagulation assessment and transplant-team approval.
